raw_result.reference_answer:
For electrochemical treatment of PFAS-contaminated landfill leachate, evaluation should explicitly go beyond reporting loss of initially targeted PFAS and include checks for precursor and product transformation signals.

On the precursor side, sulfonamide-based precursors and fluorotelomer-based precursors in landfill leachate have been reported to be electrochemically transformed into perfluoroalkyl carboxylic acids (PFCAs) during treatment, and post-treatment results showed dominance of short-chain species. This means reviewers should examine conversion of these precursors into PFCAs and track the resulting short-chain PFCAs, rather than assuming that precursor depletion implies complete removal. In particular, the extent to which short-chain PFCAs such as PFBA are degraded "has to be considered for practical purposes," so apparent precursor or parent loss should not be overinterpreted without assessing how much PFBA and other short-chain products remain.

On the product and chain-shortening side, formation of transformation products, including PFAS, is described as a well-known and unwanted issue for degradation processes, because the goal is complete PFAS mineralization. Electrochemical oxidation of landfill leachate and groundwater has been shown to form transformation products, including potentially toxic compounds that may pose environmental hazards, and advanced oxidation processes may also lead to harmful chlorinated and brominated transformation byproducts. After electrochemical treatment, short-chain PFAS can dominate the concentration profile, indicating chain-shortening that must be explicitly monitored.

Because these transformation products are not yet widely investigated and most existing studies rely on targeted triple-quadrupole PFAS quantification, which can miss many degradation byproducts, the literature highlights the need to monitor transformation products during EO treatment and stresses the importance of suspect and non-targeted screening tools. There is an urgent need for untargeted analyses to investigate how halogenated substances are formed and transformed during EO and to assess formation of possibly harmful degradation byproducts, especially in complex matrices such as landfill leachate where co-contaminants can produce an even wider range of byproducts. Thus, when reviewing electrochemical landfill-leachate treatment, one should look for evidence that precursor-to-PFCA transformations, short-chain PFAS accumulation or persistence, and a broad suite of PFAS and other halogenated transformation products have been assessed, and recognize that absence of such analyses is a key limitation on treatment claims.
